**Leonard Bernstein** ([/ˈ b ɜːr n s t aɪ n/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_BURN-styne_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-1) born **Louis Bernstein**; August 25, 1918 – October 14, 1990) was an American [conductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductor_(music) "Conductor (music)"), composer, pianist, music educator, author, and humanitarian. Considered to be one of the most important conductors of his time, he was the first American-born conductor to receive international acclaim. Bernstein was "one of the most prodigiously talented and successful musicians in American history" according to music critic [Donal Henahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donal_Henahan "Donal Henahan").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-obit-2)[Bernstein's honors and accolades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_awards_and_nominations_received_by_Leonard_Bernstein "List of awards and nominations received by Leonard Bernstein") include seven [Emmy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Awards "Emmy Awards"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-3) two [Tony Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Awards "Tony Awards"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-4) and 16 [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards") (including the [Lifetime Achievement Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award "Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award")),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-grammy-5) as well as an [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Score "Academy Award for Best Original Score") nomination. He received the [Kennedy Center Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center_Honor "Kennedy Center Honor") in 1981.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-6)

As a composer, Bernstein wrote in many genres, including symphonic and orchestral music, ballet, film and theatre music, choral works, opera, chamber music, and pieces for the piano. [Bernstein's works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_compositions_by_Leonard_Bernstein "List of compositions by Leonard Bernstein") include the [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") musical _[West Side Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West\_Side\_Story "West Side Story")_, 1957,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-7) which continues to be regularly performed worldwide, and has been adapted into two ([1961](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Side_Story_(1961_film) "West Side Story (1961 film)") and [2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Side_Story_(2021_film) "West Side Story (2021 film)")) feature films, as well as three symphonies, _[Serenade (after Plato's Symposium)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serenade\_after\_Plato's\_%22Symposium%22 "Serenade after Plato's \"Symposium\"")_ (1954) and _[Chichester Psalms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chichester\_Psalms "Chichester Psalms")_ (1965), the original score for [Elia Kazan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elia_Kazan "Elia Kazan")'s _[On the Waterfront](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_the\_Waterfront "On the Waterfront")_ (1954), and theater works including _[On the Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_the\_Town\_(musical) "On the Town (musical)")_ (1944), _[Wonderful Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonderful\_Town "Wonderful Town")_ (1953), _[Candide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candide\_(operetta) "Candide (operetta)")_ (1956), and his _[Mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass\_(Bernstein) "Mass (Bernstein)")_ (1971).

Bernstein was the first American-born conductor to lead a major American symphony orchestra.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-Oliver-8) He was music director of the [New York Philharmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Philharmonic "New York Philharmonic") and conducted the world's major orchestras, generating a legacy of audio and video recordings.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-Discography-9) Bernstein was also a critical figure in the modern revival of the music of [Gustav Mahler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Mahler "Gustav Mahler"), in whose music he was most interested.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-10) A skilled pianist,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTELaird2002[httpsbooksgooglecombooksid1aPyEzYri7UCpgPA10lpgPP1_10]-11) Bernstein often conducted piano concertos from the keyboard. He shared and explored classical music on television with a mass audience in national and international broadcasts, including [Young People's Concerts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_People's_Concerts "Young People's Concerts") with the New York Philharmonic.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-12)

Bernstein worked in support of [civil rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement "Civil rights movement");[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-Alabama-13) protested against the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War");[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-14) advocated nuclear disarmament; raised money for HIV/AIDS research and awareness; championed [Janis Ian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janis_Ian "Janis Ian") at age 15 and her song about [interracial love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interracial_marriage "Interracial marriage"), "[Society's Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society's_Child "Society's Child")", on his CBS television show; and engaged in multiple international initiatives for human rights and world peace. He conducted Mahler's _[Resurrection Symphony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resurrection\_Symphony "Resurrection Symphony")_ to mark the death of president [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy"),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-15) and in Israel at a concert, _Hatikvah on Mt. Scopus_, after the [Six-Day War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six-Day_War "Six-Day War").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-16) The sequence of events was recorded for a documentary entitled _Journey to Jerusalem_.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-17) On Christmas Day, 1989, Bernstein conducted a performance of [Beethoven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beethoven "Beethoven")'s [Symphony No. 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._9_(Beethoven) "Symphony No. 9 (Beethoven)") in Berlin to celebrate the [fall of the Berlin Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Berlin_Wall "Fall of the Berlin Wall").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-18) Less than a year later, in October 1990, he died of a heart attack in New York, aged 72.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-19)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Leonard_Bernstein&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

### 1918–1935: Early life and family

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Leonard_Bernstein&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1918–1935: Early life and family")]

Leonard Bernstein was born on August 25, 1918, in [Lawrence, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence,_Massachusetts "Lawrence, Massachusetts").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTESeldes20099-20) He was of [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish") descent.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-21)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTESeldes20099-20)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-23) His mother, Jennie ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name")Resnick),[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-Jennieobit-24) and his father, Samuel Joseph Bernstein, were both immigrants to the United States.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-Oliver-8)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTESeldes20099-20)

His father came from [Rovensky Uyezd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rovensky_Uyezd "Rovensky Uyezd") in the [Russian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire") (present-day Ukraine).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-25) Samuel was born in 1892 in an [ultra-Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra-Orthodox "Ultra-Orthodox") Jewish _[shtetl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shtetl "Shtetl")_ and wanted to become a [rabbi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabbi "Rabbi"), but after he was called up for military service, he left Russia for the United States in 1908 and initially worked at the [Fulton Fish Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulton_Fish_Market "Fulton Fish Market") in New York City.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTESeldes20099-20) Jennie was born in Russia in 1898 and arrived in the United States in 1905; she later worked at the woolen mills in Lawrence.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTESeldes20099-20)

His grandmother insisted that his first name officially be [Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_(given_name) "Louis (given name)"), but his parents always called him [Leonard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard "Leonard"). He legally changed his name to Leonard when he was 16.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeyser198722%E2%80%9323-26) To his friends and many others, he was simply known as "Lenny".[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-27)

His mother had moved in with her parents, in Lawrence, toward the end of her pregnancy with Leonard, her first child. Since he was sickly as an infant, he stayed there until he was strong enough for him and his mother to join his father in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"). There, the boy attended the [William Lloyd Garrison School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Lloyd_Garrison_School "William Lloyd Garrison School")[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-28) and then the [Boston Latin School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Latin_School "Boston Latin School"), where he and classmate Lawrence F. Ebb wrote the class song.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeyser198734%E2%80%9335-29) When Leonard was 15, the family moved to nearby [Newton, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton,_Massachusetts "Newton, Massachusetts").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-30)

Samuel became a wealthy man as the owner of the Samuel J. Bernstein Hair Company, which, in the 1920s and 1930s, held the exclusive distribution rights for the Frederick's Permanent Wave Machine.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-31)

In Leonard's early years, his main exposure to music was on Friday nights at Congregation Mishkan Tefila in the [Roxbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxbury,_Boston "Roxbury, Boston") neighborhood of Boston.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-32) Its innovative rabbi, Herman H. Rubenovitz, introduced organ music and a mixed choir to New England's Jewish congregations.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-33) He also recruited a distinguished European cantor, [Izso Glickstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izso_Glickstein "Izso Glickstein"), whom Leonard described as his _favorite cantor._[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-34) Glickstein was Burton Bernstein's godfather.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-35) Burton described Glickstein as _a cantor who could have been an opera singer_.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-36)

When Bernstein was 10 years old, his Aunt Clara, Samuel's sister, deposited her upright piano at their house. Young Bernstein asked for lessons and subsequently studied with a variety of piano teachers, including Helen Coates, who would later become his secretary.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeyser198724%E2%80%9325,_30-37) In the summers, the Bernstein family would retreat to their vacation home in [Sharon, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharon,_Massachusetts "Sharon, Massachusetts"), where Leonard conscripted all the neighborhood children to put on shows, ranging from [Bizet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bizet "Bizet")'s _[Carmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmen "Carmen")_ to [Gilbert and Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_and_Sullivan "Gilbert and Sullivan")'s _[H.M.S. Pinafore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H.M.S.\_Pinafore "H.M.S. Pinafore")_.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeyser198726,_29%E2%80%9330-38) He and his two younger siblings, Shirley and Burton, remained close their entire lives.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-39)

Samuel initially opposed Leonard's interest in music and attempted to discourage it by refusing to pay for his son's piano lessons. So, Leonard took to giving lessons to young people in his neighborhood.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-40) One of his students, [Sid Ramin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sid_Ramin "Sid Ramin"), would become a beloved lifelong friend and Bernstein's [orchestrator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestrator "Orchestrator") (along with [Irwin Kostal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irwin_Kostal "Irwin Kostal")) for _[West Side Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West\_Side\_Story "West Side Story")_.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-42)

Eventually, Samuel came around, taking his son to orchestral concerts in his teenage years and ultimately supporting his music studies, as well.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeyser198726-43) In May 1932, Leonard attended his first orchestral concert with the [Boston Pops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Pops "Boston Pops"), conducted by [Arthur Fiedler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Fiedler "Arthur Fiedler").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-44) There, Bernstein first heard [Ravel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravel "Ravel")'s _[Boléro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bol%C3%A9ro "Boléro")_, which impressed him greatly.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimeone20138-45)

On March 30, 1932, Bernstein played [Brahms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brahms "Brahms")'s [Rhapsody in G minor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhapsodies,_Op._79_(Brahms) "Rhapsodies, Op. 79 (Brahms)") at his first public piano performance in Susan Williams's studio recital at the [New England Conservatory of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Conservatory_of_Music "New England Conservatory of Music"). Two years later, he made his debut as a soloist with an orchestra, playing [Grieg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grieg "Grieg")'s [Piano Concerto in A minor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_(Grieg) "Piano Concerto (Grieg)") with the Boston Public School Orchestra.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShawn201428-46)

Among his strong musical influences was [George Gershwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Gershwin "George Gershwin"). When news came of Gershwin's death, in July 1937, Bernstein, then a music counselor at a summer camp, interrupted lunch in the mess hall and played Gershwin's second _[Prelude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three\_Preludes\_(Gershwin) "Three Preludes (Gershwin)")_ as a memorial.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-47)

### 1935–1941: College years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Leonard_Bernstein&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1935–1941: College years")]

**Harvard University**

In 1935, Bernstein enrolled at [Harvard College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_College "Harvard College"), where he studied music with, among others, composers [Edward Burlingame Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Burlingame_Hill "Edward Burlingame Hill") and [Walter Piston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Piston "Walter Piston"). Bernstein's first extant composition, [Psalm 148](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalm_148_(Bernstein) "Psalm 148 (Bernstein)"), for voice and piano, is dated 1935.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-48) He majored in music with a senior thesis titled "The Absorption of Race Elements into American Music" (1939; reproduced in his book _Findings_). One of Bernstein's intellectual influences at Harvard was [aesthetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aesthetics "Aesthetics") professor [David Prall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Prall "David Prall"), and one of his friends at the school was future philosopher [Donald Davidson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Davidson_(philosopher) "Donald Davidson (philosopher)"). Bernstein wrote and conducted the musical score for Davidson's production of the [Aristophanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristophanes "Aristophanes") play _[The Birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Birds\_(play) "The Birds (play)")_, performed in the original Greek. Bernstein recycled some of this music in future works. While a student, Bernstein composed for the [Harvard Glee Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Glee_Club "Harvard Glee Club") and was briefly its president while also serving as the unpaid pianist for Harvard Film Society's [silent film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_film "Silent film") presentations.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-49)

Bernstein mounted a student production of _[The Cradle Will Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cradle\_Will\_Rock "The Cradle Will Rock")_, directing its action from the piano as the composer [Marc Blitzstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Blitzstein "Marc Blitzstein") had done at the premiere. Blitzstein, who attended the performance, subsequently became a close friend and mentor to Bernstein.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurton199552%E2%80%9355-50) As a [sophomore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophomore "Sophomore") at Harvard, Bernstein met the conductor [Dimitri Mitropoulos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimitri_Mitropoulos "Dimitri Mitropoulos"), who was an influence on Bernstein's eventual decision to become a conductor.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurton199535%E2%80%9336-51) Mitropoulos invited Bernstein to come to [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis") for the 1940–41 season to be his assistant, but the plan fell through because of union issues.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTELairdLin2019[[Category:Wikipedia_articles_needing_page_number_citations_from_March_2022]]%3Csup_class=%22noprint_Inline-Template_%22_style=%22white-space:nowrap;%22%3E[%3Ci%3E[[Wikipedia:Citing_sources|%3Cspan_title=%22This_citation_requires_a_reference_to_the_specific_page_or_range_of_pages_in_which_the_material_appears.%20(March_2022)%22%3Epage%C2%A0needed%3C/span%3E]]%3C/i%3E]%3C/sup%3E-52) In 1937, Bernstein sat next to [Aaron Copland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Copland "Aaron Copland") at a dance recital at [Town Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Town_Hall_(New_York_City) "The Town Hall (New York City)") in New York City. Copland invited Bernstein to his birthday party afterwards, where Bernstein impressed the guests by playing Copland's challenging [Piano Variations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Variations_(Copland) "Piano Variations (Copland)"). Although he was never a formal student of Copland's, Bernstein regularly sought his advice, often citing him as "the closest thing to a composition teacher [Bernstein] ever had."[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-teachers-54) Bernstein graduated from Harvard in 1939 with a Bachelor of Arts, _[cum laude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin\_honors#United\_States "Latin honors")_.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-55)

**Curtis Institute of Music**

After graduating from Harvard, Bernstein enrolled at the [Curtis Institute of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtis_Institute_of_Music "Curtis Institute of Music") in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"). At Curtis, Bernstein studied conducting with [Fritz Reiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Reiner "Fritz Reiner"); piano with [Isabelle Vengerova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabelle_Vengerova "Isabelle Vengerova"); orchestration with [Randall Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randall_Thompson "Randall Thompson"); [counterpoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterpoint "Counterpoint") with [Richard Stöhr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_St%C3%B6hr "Richard Stöhr"); and score reading with [Renée Longy-Miquelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9e_Longy "Renée Longy").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-56) In 1940, Bernstein attended the inaugural year of the [Berkshire Music Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkshire_Music_Center "Berkshire Music Center"), the [Boston Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Symphony_Orchestra "Boston Symphony Orchestra")'s summer home.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-57) Bernstein studied conducting with the BSO's music director, [Serge Koussevitzky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serge_Koussevitzky "Serge Koussevitzky"),[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-58) who became a profound lifelong inspiration to Bernstein.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-Leonard_Bernstein_Office-59) He became Koussevitzky's conducting assistant at Tanglewood[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-Leonard_Bernstein_Office-59) and later dedicated his [Symphony No. 2: _The Age of Anxiety_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._2_(Bernstein) "Symphony No. 2 (Bernstein)") to Koussevitzky.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-60) One of Bernstein's classmates, both at Curtis and at Tanglewood, was [Lukas Foss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lukas_Foss "Lukas Foss"), who remained a lifelong friend and colleague.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-61) Bernstein returned to Tanglewood nearly every summer for the rest of his life to teach and conduct the young music students.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-62) Bernstein received a diploma in conducting from Curtis in 1941.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-63)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Leonard_Bernstein&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Career")]

### 1940s: Rise to prominence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Leonard_Bernstein&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1940s: Rise to prominence")]

Soon after he left Curtis, Bernstein moved to New York City where he lived in various apartments in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-64) Bernstein supported himself by coaching singers, teaching piano,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-Witemeyer-65) and playing the piano for dance classes in [Carnegie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall"). He found work with Harms-Witmark, transcribing jazz and pop music and publishing his work under the pseudonym "Lenny Amber". (_Bernstein_ means "[amber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amber "Amber")" in German.)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurton1995108-66)

Bernstein briefly shared an apartment in [Greenwich Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village "Greenwich Village") with his friend [Adolph Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolph_Green "Adolph Green"). Green was then part of a satirical music troupe called The Revuers, featuring [Betty Comden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Comden "Betty Comden") and [Judy Holliday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judy_Holliday "Judy Holliday"). With Bernstein sometimes providing piano accompaniment, The Revuers often performed at the legendary jazz club the [Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_Vanguard "Village Vanguard").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-68) On April 21, 1942, Bernstein performed the premiere of his first published work, _[Sonata for Clarinet and Piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonata\_for\_Clarinet\_and\_Piano\_(Bernstein) "Sonata for Clarinet and Piano (Bernstein)")_, with clarinetist David Glazer at the [Institute of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Contemporary_Art,_Boston "Institute of Contemporary Art, Boston") in Boston.

#### New York Philharmonic conducting debut

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Leonard_Bernstein&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: New York Philharmonic conducting debut")]

Bernstein would later make his New York Philharmonic conducting debut. On November 14, 1943, having recently been appointed assistant conductor to [Artur Rodziński](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artur_Rodzi%C5%84ski "Artur Rodziński") of the New York Philharmonic, Bernstein made his major conducting debut at short notice—and without any rehearsal—after guest conductor [Bruno Walter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruno_Walter "Bruno Walter") came down with the flu.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-debut-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-70) The challenging program included works by [Robert Schumann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Schumann "Robert Schumann"), [Miklós Rózsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikl%C3%B3s_R%C3%B3zsa "Miklós Rózsa"), [Richard Wagner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Wagner "Richard Wagner"), and [Richard Strauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Strauss "Richard Strauss").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-debut-69)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-71)

The next day, _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ carried the story on its front page and remarked in an editorial, "It's a good American success story. The warm, friendly triumph of it filled [Carnegie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall") and spread far over the air waves."[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-72) Many newspapers throughout the country carried the story, which, in combination with the concert's live national [CBS Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_Radio "CBS Radio") Network broadcast, propelled Bernstein to instant fame.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-73) Over the next two years, Bernstein made conducting debuts with ten different orchestras in the United States and Canada, greatly broadening his repertoire and initiating a lifelong frequent practice of conducting concertos from the piano.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurton1995142-74)

On January 28, 1944, Bernstein conducted the premiere of his [Symphony No. 1: _Jeremiah_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._1_(Bernstein) "Symphony No. 1 (Bernstein)") with the [Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Symphony_Orchestra "Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra") and soloist [Jennie Tourel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennie_Tourel "Jennie Tourel").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-75) In the fall of 1943, Bernstein and [Jerome Robbins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerome_Robbins "Jerome Robbins") began work on their first collaboration, _[Fancy Free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fancy\_Free\_(ballet) "Fancy Free (ballet)")_, a ballet about three young sailors on leave in wartime New York City. _Fancy Free_ premiered on April 18, 1944, with the [Ballet Theatre (now the American Ballet Theatre)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Ballet_Theatre "American Ballet Theatre") after completing the score only 8 days earlier at the old [Metropolitan Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Opera_House_(39th_Street) "Metropolitan Opera House (39th Street)"), with scenery by [Oliver Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Smith_(designer) "Oliver Smith (designer)") and costumes by [Kermit Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kermit_Love "Kermit Love").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-76)

Bernstein and Robbins decided to expand the ballet into a musical and invited Comden and Green to write the book and lyrics. _[On the Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_the\_Town\_(musical) "On the Town (musical)")_ opened on Broadway's [Adelphi Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelphi_Theatre "Adelphi Theatre") on December 28, 1944. The show resonated with audiences during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), and it broke race barriers on Broadway: Japanese-American dancer [Sono Osato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sono_Osato "Sono Osato") in a leading role; a multiracial cast dancing as mixed race couples; and a Black concertmaster, [Everett Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everett_Lee "Everett Lee"), who eventually took over as music director of the show.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-77)_On the Town_ became [an MGM motion picture in 1949](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Town_(film) "On the Town (film)"), starring [Gene Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Kelly "Gene Kelly"), [Frank Sinatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Sinatra "Frank Sinatra"), and [Jules Munshin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jules_Munshin "Jules Munshin") as the three sailors. Only part of Bernstein's score was used in the film and additional songs were provided by [Roger Edens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Edens "Roger Edens").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-78)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Leonard_Bernstein_NYWTS_1945.jpg/250px-Leonard_Bernstein_NYWTS_1945.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leonard_Bernstein_NYWTS_1945.jpg)

Bernstein conducting the New York City Symphony (1945)

From 1945 to 1947, Bernstein was the music director of the New York City Symphony, which had been founded the previous year by the conductor [Leopold Stokowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopold_Stokowski "Leopold Stokowski"). The orchestra (with support from Mayor Fiorello La Guardia) had modern programs and affordable tickets.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-79) In 1946, Bernstein made his overseas debut with the [Czech Philharmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Philharmonic "Czech Philharmonic") at the inaugural [Prague Spring International Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_Spring_International_Music_Festival "Prague Spring International Music Festival").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-bernstein-office-timeline-80) He also recorded Ravel's [Piano Concerto in G major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_in_G_major_(Ravel) "Piano Concerto in G major (Ravel)") as soloist and conductor with the [Philharmonia Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philharmonia_Orchestra "Philharmonia Orchestra").[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-81) On July 4, 1946, Bernstein conducted the European premiere of _Fancy Free_ with the Ballet Theatre at the [Royal Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Opera_House "Royal Opera House") in London.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-82) On August 6 he conducted opera professionally for the first time, with the American premiere of [Benjamin Britten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Britten "Benjamin Britten")'s _[Peter Grimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter\_Grimes "Peter Grimes")_ at Tanglewood, commissioned by Koussevitzky.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-83) That same year, [Arturo Toscanini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Toscanini "Arturo Toscanini") invited Bernstein to guest conduct two concerts with the [NBC Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_Symphony_Orchestra "NBC Symphony Orchestra"), one of which featured Bernstein as soloist in Ravel's Piano Concerto in G major.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-84)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_]

#### Israel Philharmonic Orchestra, television debut and Tanglewood

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Leonard_Bernstein&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Israel Philharmonic Orchestra, television debut and Tanglewood")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Leonard_Bernstein%2C_1953_-_collezione_Tino_Barindelli.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Leonard_Bernstein%2C_1953_-_collezione_Tino_Barindelli.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leonard_Bernstein,_1953_-_collezione_Tino_Barindelli.tif)

Leonard Bernstein (photo with dedication from 1953)

In 1947, Bernstein conducted in [Tel Aviv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Aviv "Tel Aviv") for the first time, beginning a lifelong association with the [Israel Philharmonic Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Philharmonic_Orchestra "Israel Philharmonic Orchestra"), then known as the Palestine Symphony Orchestra. The next year, he conducted an open-air concert for Israeli troops at [Beersheba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beersheba "Beersheba") in the middle of the desert during the [Arab-Israeli war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab%E2%80%93Israeli_conflict "Arab–Israeli conflict").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-85) In 1957, he conducted the inaugural concert of the [Mann Auditorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mann_Auditorium "Mann Auditorium") in Tel Aviv.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-bernstein-office-timeline-80) In 1967, he conducted a concert on [Mount Scopus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Scopus "Mount Scopus") to commemorate the [Reunification of Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reunification_of_Jerusalem "Reunification of Jerusalem"), featuring [Mahler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler "Mahler")'s [Symphony No. 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._2_(Mahler) "Symphony No. 2 (Mahler)") and [Mendelssohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendelssohn "Mendelssohn")'s [Violin Concerto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn) "Violin Concerto (Mendelssohn)") with soloist [Isaac Stern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Stern "Isaac Stern").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-86) The city of Tel Aviv added his name to the [Habima Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habima_Square "Habima Square") (Orchestra Plaza) in the center of the city.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-87) On December 10, 1949, Bernstein made his first television appearance as conductor with the [Boston Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Symphony_Orchestra "Boston Symphony Orchestra") at [Carnegie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall"). The concert, which included an address by [Eleanor Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleanor_Roosevelt "Eleanor Roosevelt"), celebrated the first anniversary of the [United Nations General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly")'s ratification of the [Universal Declaration of Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Declaration_of_Human_Rights "Universal Declaration of Human Rights"), and included the premiere of [Aaron Copland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Copland "Aaron Copland")'s _Preamble for a Solemn Occasion_ with [Laurence Olivier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Olivier "Laurence Olivier") narrating text from the [UN Charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_Charter "UN Charter"). The concert was televised by [NBC Television Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_Television_Network "NBC Television Network").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-88) In April 1949, Bernstein performed as piano soloist in the world premiere of his [Symphony No. 2: The Age of Anxiety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._2_(Bernstein) "Symphony No. 2 (Bernstein)") with Koussevitzy conducting the Boston Symphony Orchestra. On December 2, 1949, Bernstein conducted the world premiere of the [Messiaen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messiaen "Messiaen")'s _[Turangalîla-Symphonie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turangal%C3%AEla-Symphonie "Turangalîla-Symphonie")_, with the Boston Symphony Orchestra and the New York premiere in Carnegie Hall on the afternoon of December 10.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-89) Part of the rehearsal for the concert was recorded and released by the orchestra. When Koussevitzky died in 1951, Bernstein became head of the orchestra and conducting departments at [Tanglewood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanglewood_Music_Festival "Tanglewood Music Festival").

### 1950s: Career expansion and _West Side Story_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Leonard_Bernstein&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1950s: Career expansion and West Side Story")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Leonard_Bernstein_-_1950s.JPG/250px-Leonard_Bernstein_-_1950s.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leonard_Bernstein_-_1950s.JPG)

Bernstein, c. 1950s

The 1950s comprised the most active years of Bernstein's career. He created five new works for the Broadway stage, composed several symphonic works and an iconic film score, and was appointed music director of the New York Philharmonic with whom he toured the world, including concerts behind the Iron Curtain. Bernstein also harnessed the power of television to expand his educational reach, and he married and started a family. In 1950, Bernstein composed incidental music for a Broadway production of J. M. Barrie's play _[Peter Pan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter\_Pan\_(1950\_musical) "Peter Pan (1950 musical)")_.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-90) The production, which opened on Broadway on April 24, 1950, starred [Jean Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Arthur "Jean Arthur") as [Peter Pan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Pan_(character) "Peter Pan (character)") and [Boris Karloff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Karloff "Boris Karloff") in the dual roles of [George Darling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Darling_(Peter_Pan) "George Darling (Peter Pan)") and [Captain Hook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Hook "Captain Hook"). The show ran for 321 performances.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-91)

In 1951, Bernstein composed _[Trouble in Tahiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trouble\_in\_Tahiti "Trouble in Tahiti")_, a one-act opera in seven scenes with an English [libretto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libretto "Libretto") by the composer. The opera portrays the troubled marriage of a couple whose idyllic suburban post-war environment belies their inner turmoil.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-92) Ironically, Bernstein wrote most of the opera while on his honeymoon in Mexico with his wife, [Felicia Montealegre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felicia_Montealegre "Felicia Montealegre")-Cohn. Bernstein was a visiting music professor at [Brandeis University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandeis_University "Brandeis University") from 1951 to 1956. In 1952, he created the [Brandeis Festival of the Creative Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein_Festival_of_the_Creative_Arts "Leonard Bernstein Festival of the Creative Arts"), where he conducted the premiere of _[Trouble in Tahiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trouble\_in\_Tahiti "Trouble in Tahiti")_ on June 12 of that year.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-93) The [NBC Opera Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_Opera_Theatre "NBC Opera Theatre") subsequently presented the opera on television in November 1952. It opened on Broadway at the Playhouse Theatre on April 19, 1955, and ran for six weeks.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-94) Three decades later, Bernstein wrote a second opera, _[A Quiet Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Quiet\_Place\_(opera) "A Quiet Place (opera)")_ (1983), which picked up the story and characters of _Trouble in Tahiti_ in a later period.

Bernstein collaborated with [Comden and Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comden_and_Green "Comden and Green") on _[Wonderful Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonderful\_Town "Wonderful Town")_

**_Wonderful Town_ (1953)**

Main article: [Wonderful Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonderful_Town "Wonderful Town")

In 1953, Bernstein wrote the score for the musical _[Wonderful Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonderful\_Town "Wonderful Town")_ on very short notice, with a book by [Joseph A. Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_A._Fields "Joseph A. Fields") and [Jerome Chodorov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerome_Chodorov "Jerome Chodorov") and lyrics by [Betty Comden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Comden "Betty Comden") and [Adolph Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolph_Green "Adolph Green"). Like the 1940 play, directed on Broadway by [George S. Kaufman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_S._Kaufman "George S. Kaufman"), it is based on the autobiographical short stories, collectively titled _[My Sister Eileen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Sister\_Eileen\_(play) "My Sister Eileen (play)")_, that were written by [Ruth McKenney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_McKenney "Ruth McKenney") and published in the early 1930s by _[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_. They tell the story of two sisters from Ohio who move to New York City and seek success from their squalid [basement apartment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basement_apartment "Basement apartment") in [Greenwich Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village "Greenwich Village"). _Wonderful Town_ opened on [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") on February 25, 1953, at the [Winter Garden Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Garden_Theatre "Winter Garden Theatre"), starring [Rosalind Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosalind_Russell "Rosalind Russell") in the role of Ruth Sherwood, [Edie Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edie_Adams "Edie Adams") as Eileen Sherwood, and [George Gaynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Gaynes "George Gaynes") as Robert Baker. It won five [Tony Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Awards "Tony Awards"), including Best Musical and Best Actress.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-95)

**_Candide_ (1956)**

Main article: [Candide (operetta)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candide_(operetta) "Candide (operetta)")

In the three years leading up to Bernstein's appointment as music director of the New York Philharmonic, Bernstein was simultaneously working on the scores for two Broadway shows. The first of the two was the [operetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operetta "Operetta")-style musical _[Candide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candide\_(operetta) "Candide (operetta)")._[Lillian Hellman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lillian_Hellman "Lillian Hellman") originally brought Bernstein her idea of adapting [Voltaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voltaire "Voltaire")'s [novella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candide "Candide").[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimeone2013311-96) The original collaborators on the show were book writer [John Latouche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_La_Touche_(lyricist) "John La Touche (lyricist)") and lyricist [Richard Wilbur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Wilbur "Richard Wilbur"). _Candide_ opened on [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") on December 1, 1956, at the [Martin Beck Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Beck_Theatre "Martin Beck Theatre"), in a production directed by [Tyrone Guthrie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrone_Guthrie "Tyrone Guthrie"). Anxious about the parallels Hellman had deliberately drawn between Voltaire's story and the ongoing hearings conducted by the [House Un-American Activities Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Un-American_Activities_Committee "House Un-American Activities Committee"), Guthrie persuaded the collaborators to cut their most incendiary sections prior to opening night.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurton1995260-97) While the production was a box office disaster, running for only two months for a total of 73 performances,[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-98) the cast album became a cult classic, which kept Bernstein's score alive. There have been several revivals, with modifications to improve the book. The elements of the music that have remained best known and performed over the decades are the Overture, which quickly became one of the most frequently performed orchestral compositions by a [20th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th-century_classical_music "20th-century classical music")[American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_the_United_States "Music of the United States") composer; the coloratura aria "Glitter and Be Gay", which [Barbara Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Cook "Barbara Cook") sang in the original production; and the grand finale "Make Our Garden Grow".

**_West Side Story_ (1957)**

Main article: [West Side Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Side_Story "West Side Story")

The other musical Bernstein was writing simultaneously with _Candide_ was _[West Side Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West\_Side\_Story "West Side Story")_. Bernstein collaborated with director and choreographer [Jerome Robbins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerome_Robbins "Jerome Robbins"), book writer [Arthur Laurents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Laurents "Arthur Laurents"), and lyricist [Stephen Sondheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Sondheim "Stephen Sondheim").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-99) The story is an updated retelling of [Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare "Shakespeare")'s _[Romeo and Juliet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romeo\_and\_Juliet "Romeo and Juliet")_, set in the mid-1950s in the slums of New York City's [Upper West Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_West_Side "Upper West Side"). The Romeo character, Tony, is affiliated with the Jets gang, who are of white Northern European descent. The Juliet character is Maria, who is connected to the Sharks gang, recently arrived from [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-100) The original Broadway production opened at the [Winter Garden Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Garden_Theatre "Winter Garden Theatre") on September 26, 1957, and ran 732 performances. Robbins won the [Tony Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Award "Tony Award") for Best Choreographer, and [Oliver Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Smith_(designer) "Oliver Smith (designer)") won the Tony for Best Scenic Designer.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-101)

Bernstein's score for _West Side Story_ blends "jazz, Latin rhythms, symphonic sweep and musical-comedy conventions in groundbreaking ways for Broadway".[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-102) It was [orchestrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestrated "Orchestrated") by [Sid Ramin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sid_Ramin "Sid Ramin") and [Irwin Kostal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irwin_Kostal "Irwin Kostal") following detailed instructions from Bernstein. The dark theme, sophisticated music, extended dance scenes, and focus on social problems marked a turning point in musical theatre. In 1960, Bernstein prepared a [suite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suite_(music) "Suite (music)") of orchestral music from the show, titled _Symphonic Dances from West Side Story_, which continues to be popular with orchestras worldwide.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-103) A [1961 United Artists film adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Side_Story_(1961_film) "West Side Story (1961 film)"), directed by [Robert Wise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wise "Robert Wise") and Robbins, starred [Natalie Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natalie_Wood "Natalie Wood") as Maria and [Richard Beymer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Beymer "Richard Beymer") as Tony. The film won ten [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards"), including [Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture") and a ground-breaking Best Supporting Actress award for Puerto Rican-born [Rita Moreno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Moreno "Rita Moreno") playing the role of Anita.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-104) A [film adaptation directed by Steven Spielberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Side_Story_(2021_film) "West Side Story (2021 film)") opened in 2021.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-105)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/I_Feel_Pretty_from_West_Side_Story_1957.JPG/330px-I_Feel_Pretty_from_West_Side_Story_1957.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:I_Feel_Pretty_from_West_Side_Story_1957.JPG)

L–R: [Elizabeth Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Taylor_Davis "Frances Taylor Davis"),[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-106) Carmen Gutierrez, [Marilyn Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Cooper "Marilyn Cooper"), and [Carol Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Lawrence "Carol Lawrence") from the original Broadway cast sing "[I Feel Pretty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Feel_Pretty "I Feel Pretty")" (1957)

In addition to Bernstein's compositional activity for the stage, he wrote a symphonic work, _[Serenade after Plato's "Symposium"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serenade\_after\_Plato's\_%22Symposium%22 "Serenade after Plato's \"Symposium\"")_ (1954); the score _[On the Waterfront](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_the\_Waterfront "On the Waterfront")_ (1954); and _[Prelude, Fugue and Riffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prelude,\_Fugue\_and\_Riffs "Prelude, Fugue and Riffs")_, composed in 1949, but only premiered in 1955, for jazz big band and solo clarinet. In 1953, Bernstein became the first American conductor to appear at [La Scala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Scala "La Scala") in Milan, conducting Cherubini's _[Medea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9d%C3%A9e\_(Cherubini) "Médée (Cherubini)")_, with [Maria Callas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Callas "Maria Callas") in the title role. Callas and Bernstein reunited at La Scala to perform Bellini's _[La sonnambula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_sonnambula "La sonnambula")_ in 1955. On November 14, 1954, Bernstein presented the first of his television lectures for the CBS Television Network arts program _[Omnibus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omnibus\_(American\_TV\_program) "Omnibus (American TV program)")_. The live lecture, entitled "Beethoven's Fifth Symphony", involved Bernstein explaining the symphony's first movement with the aid of musicians from the "Symphony of the Air" (formerly [NBC Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_Symphony_Orchestra "NBC Symphony Orchestra")). The program featured manuscripts from Beethoven's own hand, as well as a giant painting of the first page of the score covering the studio floor. Six more _Omnibus_ lectures followed from 1955 to 1961 (later on ABC and then NBC) covering a broad range of topics: jazz, conducting, American musical comedy, modern music, [J. S. Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._S._Bach "J. S. Bach"), and [grand opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_opera "Grand opera").

**Music director of the New York Philharmonic**

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Leonard_Bernstein_NYWTS_1955.jpg/250px-Leonard_Bernstein_NYWTS_1955.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leonard_Bernstein_NYWTS_1955.jpg)

Bernstein at the piano, annotating a musical score, 1955

Bernstein was appointed the music director of the New York Philharmonic in 1957, sharing the post jointly with [Dimitri Mitropoulos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimitri_Mitropoulos "Dimitri Mitropoulos") until he took sole charge in 1958. Bernstein held the music directorship until 1969 when he was appointed "Laureate Conductor". He continued to conduct and make recordings with the orchestra for the rest of his life.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-107) Bernstein's television teaching took a quantum leap when, as the new music director of the New York Philharmonic, he put the orchestra's traditional Saturday afternoon [Young People's Concerts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_People's_Concerts "Young People's Concerts") on the CBS Television Network. Millions of viewers of all ages and around the world enthusiastically embraced Bernstein and his engaging presentations about classical music. Bernstein often presented talented young performers on the broadcasts. Many of them became celebrated in their own right, including conductors [Claudio Abbado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudio_Abbado "Claudio Abbado") and [Seiji Ozawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seiji_Ozawa "Seiji Ozawa"); flutist [Paula Robison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Robison "Paula Robison"); and pianist [André Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Watts "André Watts"). From 1958 until 1972, the 53 Young People's Concerts comprised the most influential series of music education programs ever produced on television.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-108) They were highly acclaimed by critics and won numerous [Emmy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Awards "Emmy Awards").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-109)

Some of Bernstein's scripts, all of which he wrote himself, were released in book form and on records.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-110) A recording of _Humor in Music_ was awarded a [Grammy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy "Grammy") award for Best Documentary or Spoken Word Recording (other than comedy) in 1961.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-111) The programs were shown in many countries around the world, often with Bernstein dubbed into other languages, and the concerts were later released on home video by [Kultur Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kultur_Video "Kultur Video").

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Bernstein_with_TV_Camera.jpg/250px-Bernstein_with_TV_Camera.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bernstein_with_TV_Camera.jpg)

Bernstein with members of the New York Philharmonic rehearsing for a television broadcast, c.1958

In 1958, Bernstein and Mitropoulos led the New York Philharmonic on its first tour south of the border, through 12 countries in Central and South America. The [United States Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State") sponsored the tour to improve the nation's relations with its southern neighbors.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTELairdLin2019[[Category:Wikipedia_articles_needing_page_number_citations_from_March_2022]]%3Csup_class=%22noprint_Inline-Template_%22_style=%22white-space:nowrap;%22%3E[%3Ci%3E[[Wikipedia:Citing_sources|%3Cspan_title=%22This_citation_requires_a_reference_to_the_specific_page_or_range_of_pages_in_which_the_material_appears.%20(March_2022)%22%3Epage%C2%A0needed%3C/span%3E]]%3C/i%3E]%3C/sup%3E-52) In 1959, the Department of State also sponsored Bernstein and the Philharmonic on a 50-concert tour through Europe and the Soviet Union, portions of which were filmed by the [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS") Television Network. A highlight of the tour was Bernstein's performance of [Shostakovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shostakovich "Shostakovich")'s [Fifth Symphony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._5_(Shostakovich) "Symphony No. 5 (Shostakovich)"), in the presence of the composer, who came on stage at the end to congratulate Bernstein and the musicians.

### 1960s: Innovations and Lincoln Center

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Leonard_Bernstein&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 1960s: Innovations and Lincoln Center")]

**New York Philharmonic Innovations**

Bernstein's innovative approach to themed programming included introducing audiences to composers less-performed at the time such as [Gustav Mahler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Mahler "Gustav Mahler"), [Carl Nielsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Nielsen "Carl Nielsen"), [Jean Sibelius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Sibelius "Jean Sibelius"), and [Charles Ives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Ives "Charles Ives") (including the world premiere of his [Symphony No. 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._2_(Ives) "Symphony No. 2 (Ives)")). Bernstein actively advocated for the commission and performance of works by contemporary composers, conducting over 40 world premieres by a diverse roster of composers ranging from [John Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage "John Cage") to [Alberto Ginastera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_Ginastera "Alberto Ginastera") to [Luciano Berio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Berio "Luciano Berio").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-112) He also conducted US premieres of 19 major works from around the globe, including works by [Dmitri Shostakovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Shostakovich "Dmitri Shostakovich"), [Pierre Boulez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Boulez "Pierre Boulez"), and [György Ligeti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gy%C3%B6rgy_Ligeti "György Ligeti").[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-113)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Leonard-Bernstein-1959.jpg/250px-Leonard-Bernstein-1959.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leonard-Bernstein-1959.jpg)

Bernstein during a visit to Finland, 1959

Bernstein championed American composers, especially those with whom he had a close friendship, such as [Aaron Copland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Copland "Aaron Copland"), [William Schuman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Schuman "William Schuman"), and [David Diamond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Diamond_(composer) "David Diamond (composer)"). This decade saw a significant expansion of Bernstein and the Philharmonic's collaboration with [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"), together they released over 400 compositions, covering a broad swath of the classical music canon. Bernstein welcomed the Philharmonic's additions of its first Black musician, [Sanford Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanford_Allen "Sanford Allen"), and its second woman musician, [Orin O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orin_O'Brien "Orin O'Brien"). Bernstein also shared the Philharmonic's commitment to connecting with as many New Yorkers as possible. That vision became a reality with the launch of the Concerts in the Parks in 1965, which Bernstein conducted often. Another milestone was the Philharmonic's first visit to Japan in 1961, when Bernstein led acclaimed Philharmonic concerts and engaged in cultural exchange. Over the years, he led the Orchestra on tours to 144 cities in 38 countries.

Bernstein initiated the Philharmonic's informal Thursday Evening Preview Concerts, which included Bernstein's talks from the stage, a practice that was unheard of at the time.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-114)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-115) In one oft-reported incident, on April 6, 1962,[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-116) Bernstein appeared on stage before [a performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Philharmonic_concert_of_April_6,_1962 "New York Philharmonic concert of April 6, 1962") of the [Brahms Piano Concerto No. 1 in D minor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Brahms) "Piano Concerto No. 1 (Brahms)") to explain that the soloist, [Glenn Gould](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Gould "Glenn Gould"), had chosen an idiosyncratic approach to the work. Bernstein explained that while he did not totally agree with it, he thought Gould's interpretation was an artistically worthy exploration.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-117) Bernstein questioned: "In a concerto, who is the boss: the soloist or the conductor?"[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-118) The incident created a stir that reverberated in the press for decades; see [New York Philharmonic concert of April 6, 1962 §Legacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Philharmonic_concert_of_April_6,_1962#Legacy "New York Philharmonic concert of April 6, 1962").

In 1960, Bernstein and the New York Philharmonic marked the centennial of Gustav Mahler's birth with a series of performances. The composer's widow, [Alma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alma_Mahler "Alma Mahler"), attended some of Bernstein's rehearsals. That same year, Bernstein made his first commercial recording of a [Mahler symphony (the Fourth)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._4_(Mahler) "Symphony No. 4 (Mahler)"). Over the next seven years, he recorded the entire [Mahler symphony cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%E2%80%93Mahler_cycle "Bernstein–Mahler cycle") with the New York Philharmonic (except for [the 8th Symphony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Mahler) "Symphony No. 8 (Mahler)"), which was recorded with the [London Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Symphony_Orchestra "London Symphony Orchestra")). The combination of concert performances, television talks, and recordings led to a renewed interest in Mahler, especially in the United States.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-119) Bernstein claimed that he identified with the works on a personal level, and once wrote of the composer: "I'm so sympathetic to Mahler: I understand his problem. It's like being two different men locked up in the same body; one man is a conductor and the other a composer ... It's like being a double man."[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-120)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein#cite_note-121)
